rows.subtype: Approach: researching the person before writing [Thinking]
rows.description: Before messaging an engineer at a target company, the student reads their posts and finds one talk they gave, so the message can ask something specific and respectful.

rows.subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of the call [Thinking]
rows.description: The student rehearses the opening line and two questions, and imagines the call going quiet, so nerves feel less like a threat when the real call starts.

rows.subtype: Approach: asking for a job in the first message [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student writes to a stranger, asking straight away for a referral, and the message goes unanswered because there is no relationship or context to justify the favour.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing what went wrong after silence [Revision]
rows.description: After five ignored messages, the student shows the drafts to a senior, who points out that they are long and vague. The rewrite gets two replies.

rows.subtype: Approach: clarifying own values and comfort level [Thinking]
rows.description: A teen asks herself what she is comfortable with in a friendship or crush, such as sharing photos or meeting alone, and writes limits down before the situation arises.

rows.subtype: Approach: stating a boundary clearly and calmly [Action]
rows.description: A student tells someone he likes that he is not ready to share private pictures or meet alone, using simple direct words, and does not apologise for the limit.

rows.subtype: Approach: giving in to avoid losing the relationship [Pitfall]
rows.description: A teen shares private photos because he says everyone does and he will leave otherwise, valuing the relationship over comfort, and later fears where the photos might travel.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing the boundary after new information [Revision]
rows.description: After some months of trust, a teen adjusts what she shares with a close friend but keeps the core limits, showing that boundaries can shift with time without dropping her own comfort.

rows.subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations
rows.subtype: Approach: listing shared values and non-negotiables with the partner [Thinking]
rows.description: A couple writes what matters to each: a small ceremony, both families comfortable, and no debt. This list becomes the filter for every later choice.

rows.subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations
rows.subtype: Approach: budgeting with fixed caps per category [Action]
rows.description: They set a total, split it for venue, food, clothes and rituals, and keep a shared sheet. When the caterer costs more, they trim the guest list instead of borrowing.

rows.subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations
rows.subtype: Approach: giving in to every relative's demand [Pitfall]
rows.description: Trying to keep everyone happy, they add guests, events and expensive rituals. The budget doubles, the couple feels the event is no longer theirs, and stress strains their relationship.

rows.subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations
rows.subtype: Approach: pausing to reset after a conflict over guests [Revision]
rows.description: After a heated fight over the guest list, they step back, agree on a cap and a rule for exceptions, and explain it kindly to both families with the reasons.

rows.subtype: Approach: follow official warnings and evacuation orders [Action]
rows.description: When flood alerts are issued for a river town, a student checks the district authority and weather department updates and moves to a designated shelter early. Official information beats rumours.

rows.subtype: Approach: scenario planning for power and phone loss [Thinking]
rows.description: The person imagines being cut off for two days and plans for a paper list of numbers, a radio or offline map, and a shared plan on who contacts whom. Contingency thinking covers what technology may not.

rows.subtype: Approach: wait and see because it may not be serious [Pitfall]
rows.description: Having seen earlier warnings pass with little harm, the person stays put until water enters the ground floor. Normalcy bias delays leaving until the routes are cut.

rows.subtype: Approach: rebuild with documents, insurance and mental-health support [Revision]
rows.description: After the disaster, the person applies for relief, files an insurance claim with photos, replaces lost papers and speaks to a counsellor about stress. Recovery is planned in stages.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from a target role [Thinking]
rows.description: A developer aiming to become an architect by twenty-nine lists what that role needs, such as system design, leading a team and domain depth, then assigns each to a year.

rows.subtype: Approach: yearly themes with quarterly goals [Action]
rows.description: Year one focuses on core skills, year two on ownership of a module, and so on. Each quarter has one or two measurable goals, reviewed in a short written note.

rows.subtype: Approach: following the highest salary each time [Pitfall]
rows.description: The person hops to whichever company pays most, ignoring learning and reputation. After four years the resume shows many names but little depth or a clear direction.

rows.subtype: Approach: annual review and replan [Revision]
rows.description: Each December the person compares results with the plan, drops goals that no longer fit, adds new ones based on the market and personal life, and records why.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from promotion criteria [Thinking]
rows.description: An analyst reads the senior-level criteria and compares them to her record. She sees she lacks cross-team ownership, so she plans a project that builds that evidence over two quarters.

rows.subtype: Approach: asking the manager for explicit expectations [Action]
rows.description: He asks directly what a promotion would require and by when. The manager names three gaps, and they agree to review progress every month.

rows.subtype: Approach: waiting to be noticed for hard work [Pitfall]
rows.description: She assumes long hours will speak for themselves and never discusses her goal. The committee sees a reliable employee but no case for a bigger role, and a colleague who asked is promoted.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing feedback and adjusting the timeline [Revision]
rows.description: When the manager says leadership skills are not yet shown, he lets go of the current cycle. He plans to mentor an intern and lead a demo, and targets the next cycle.
